title: Dirksen: A champion in advancing civil rights
author: DAVID REEL
content:
Dirksen: A champion in advancing civil rights

 June 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 793
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On June 19 every year, Americans observe Juneteenth. It is a civil rights milestone in remembrance of an order issued in Texas in 1865 to enforce Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.Nearly a century later another civil rights milestone occurred in the United States Senate.
In the early morning hours of June 11, 1964, senators approved a cloture motion that effectively ended further debate on legislation to extend civil, political and legal rights to Black Americans. It was one of the most meaningful pieces of civil rights legislation since the 12-year Reconstruction Era immediately following the end of the American Civil War.
Today a largely forgotten unsung hero on that issue was conservative Republican Sen. Everett McKinley Dirksen of Illinois. At the time, Dirksen was the minority floor leader.
In February 1964, the U.S. House approved a civil rights bill originally proposed by former President Kennedy. The bill immediately encountered fierce opposition primarily, but not exclusively, from Democratic U.S. senators from Southern states. Unable to kill the bill in the House, their strategy was simple — ensure there would not be 67 senators to vote for cloture to close off debate on the House bill and ensure there would not be a majority of senators to vote aye on passage of the House bill if that bill ever did make it to the Senate floor.
Early in the debate, Democratic Senate Majority Leader Kike Mansfield and Democratic Sen. Hubert Humprey (the floor leader on the bill) reached the same conclusion — Republican Sen. Dirksen would be a pivotal player in providing enough Republican votes to end the debate and pass the bill.
Mansfield said candidly and prophetically, "The key is Dirksen."
Prior to his assassination, Democratic President Kennedy concurred with that assessment. Democratic President Johnson did as well after succeeding Kennedy.
Initially, Dirksen could only guarantee that 12 to 14 of his 33 Republicans would join with 41 Democratic senators. Even with those combined votes, proponents of the bill were still short of the votes necessary to shut down the opposition efforts led by Southern Democratic senators.
Dirksen soon rose to the occasion. He was the right man in the right place, at the right time.
Dirksen was a pragmatic politician and took the "big view" of his position as Senate minority Leader. He knew taking hard line partisan stances would not be good for America.
Dirksen also knew that the bill as written when it passed the House was dead on arrival in the Senate.
Undaunted by long odds and despite serious health issues, Dirksen rewrote the bill with the help of several legal experts. Together they came up with almost 70 amendments all designed to fashion a bill that could get enough votes in the Senate to end a filibuster, get enough votes to be approved in the Senate, get enough votes in the House to concur with the Senate version of the original House bill, and be signed into law by the president.
Dirksen's revised bill was not a perfect bill. None ever are. It did honor the timeless approach for progress in the legislative arena — acknowledging that success ultimately results from focusing on the art of the possible.
On June 10, 1964, Dirksen's strategy was put to test. Immediately after the original House bill was brought forward for Senate debate and consideration, West Virginia's Democratic Sen. Robert Byrd launched a speech in opposition. That speech lasted over 14 hours. Following Byrd was Georgia's Democratic Sen. Richard Russell, a decades long leader of Southern states opposition to federal civil rights legislation.
Eventually Dirksen spoke on his revised bill. He put country first and political party second.
Dirksen said, "The time has come for equality of opportunity in sharing in government, in education and in employment. It will not be stayed or denied. It is here." For emphasis, he included Victor Hugo's quote: "Stronger than all the armies is an idea whose time has come."
Dirksen's amendment strategy, his unwavering commitment to doing the right thing and his eloquence worked.
Twenty-three Republican senators voted to close debate. They also voted for his bill resulting in a final approval vote of 71 ayes and only 29 nays. Given that level of Senate support the House quickly agreed to Dirksen's version of their original bill.
On July 2, 1964, President Johnson signed the bill that banned discrimination in public facilities, provided voting rights protection and established equal opportunity as the law of the land.
Time magazine (coincidentally published on June 19, 1964), included Dirksen's picture and the following observation on their front cover: "The Civil Rights Bill Product of Principle and Compromise."
With all due respect to Juneteenth, I suggest June is also an appropriate time to ensure Everett Dirksen is not forgotten as a champion in advancing civil rights in America.
David Reel is a public affairs and public relations consultant in Easton.

title: Quiet majority of concerned citizens
author: Staff Writer
content:
Quiet majority of concerned citizens

 June 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 379
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As I have been following the recent issues related to the recent Pride festival with flags posted around town, I am writing in support of Easton Town Council President Mr. Gunsallus and member Mr. Montgomery both of whom seem to have acquired minimal support so far.It appears Mr. Gunsallus' statement regarding the posting of the Pride rainbow flags around town was not a good idea. He stated that the Pride flag was "antithetical to America" and that he believes "that it is a socialist endeavor parading beyond or behind the guise of a socialist movement, and I think that we should not be using taxpayer funds to support a cause that is antithetical (in stark contrast to) our country and our principles and our Constitution."
Mr. Montgomery voiced support, and so do I and the majority of people I am acquainted with. I've been been appalled at the negative responses of the LBGTQ community and their supporters since this happened and the vitriol which Mr. Gunsallus has been subjected to from this loud and angry societal fringe of people who supposedly stand for freedom.
I am a proud white, English-American, evangelical Christian, heterosexual, mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, nurse, teacher and fervent American patriot. But I do not feel the need to publicly celebrate with flags celebrating any of these titles. The American flag covers them all, including the LGBTQs of the country, and is all that is needed to fly in the cities, towns and villages of our country as it stands for freedom for all.
Unfortunately this fringe community has a goal of determination to legitimize and normalize their deviant lifestyle choices by forcing those with differing beliefs, especially those based on biblical standards, not only to validate but to celebrate these choices. They represent less than 20% of the population, yet they insist that diversity, equity and inclusion requires everyone to not only agree with them but celebrate them and their aggressive agenda.
Mr. Gunsallus is like the boy who recognized that "the emperor has no clothes" pointing out the absurdity of this agenda which only serves to divide us. He and Mr. Montgomery should be applauded for their boldness and not allow themselves to be overcome by the noise.
There is a quiet majority of concerned citizens behind them.
LINDA HOUCHENS
St. Michaels

title: First Frederick Douglass Unity Day held to raise money for cultural center
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
First Frederick Douglass Unity Day held to raise money for cultural center

 July 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As DJ Mercury played music outside the Easton Veterans of Foreign Wars post during the first Frederick Douglass Unity Day celebration on Saturday, people danced and feasted on crabs and corn on the cob.The event, sponsored by the Bailey-Groce Family Foundation, brought multiple vendors and somewhere around 100 people out to the VFW Saturday. It was put on to raise awareness for and money to create an African American cultural center in Easton.
Tarence Bailey, who helped organize the event, said Talbot County should be one of the first places people think of when it comes to African American history. He called the Eastern Shore a "holy ground" for Black history and said the county should have a facility to preserve that history.
"There's no getting around it," he said. "It's got to be preserved."
Bailey said it's important that the cultural center goes in The Hill Community in Easton, which is a free African American community that has been around for over 200 years.
"Because how do you preserve a community if you're not in it?" he said.
Once created, the center would showcase African American culture and history. Plans for the center include lecture halls, small business incubators and a trade department. Bailey said he wants it to be an epicenter for Black history and culture.
There are also plans to restore a property in The Hill on South Street.
"We want to do an agreement where we're going to restore the house back to period and then it can be a part of the Hill tour," he said.
Bailey thinks the the South Street property would compliment a cultural center.
"So when you go in the cultural center you see the history," he said. "(And then) there be an actual place where you can go and look at the house that was back to period of when the Hill first started."
Ashley Chenault, who owns the property, said Bailey brought the idea to her.
"But I was looking for a way to restore the home and provide community access and something for the community," she said. "So (I) really found it to be a great partnership."
Chenault, who was at the event on Saturday, said she was having a great time. She said she enjoyed eating crabs, socializing and listening to good music.
India Thomas of Thomas Family Catering, who catered the event, said it was a good day.
Thomas and her crew made fish, chicken and barbecue chicken at the event on Saturday. She said that events like these bring everyone together.
"There's enough separation in the world," she said.
Bailey, who called the event "a lot of hard work," said the people who came out made the day a special one.
"Seeing people actually enjoying the hard work and supporting the Eastern Shore family of Frederick Douglass," he said is what he enjoyed most.
Bailey hopes to make the event, which fell on the weekend between Juneteenth and Fourth of July, a bigger one next year.
"This is a good event to bring people together," he said. "This is a great middle ground."

title: 'Pride goes before destruction'
author: Staff Writer
content:
'Pride goes before destruction'

 July 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 383
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I take issue with two significant arguments in two letters published in the July 7 paper. Numerous individuals present these arguments, beyond the two letter senders. But they are wrong and dangerous. They contribute to the divisions in the country.One writer claims to be a proud, white, American, Christian, heterosexual, parent, grandparent, etc. Her pride in belonging to privileged groups is weaponized against those who make what she calls "deviant" life choices.
The writer should read the Bible.
Proverbs 16:18: "Pride goes before destruction..." The seven deadly sins go back in Christian tradition to Pope Gregory I. The worst of the deadly sins is pride. Pride places one above God. The writer asserts her pride in being white, American, Christian and heterosexual, seemingly dismissing any contributions by God. She did not make herself. God made her. And God made those she dislikes. She isn't better than them.
Pride is an excessive focus on oneself at the expense of others. It is evil. It fosters a mentality of "us" versus "them."
Another writer puts the "us" vs. "them" distinction in terms of insiders vs. outsiders. The Eastern Shore has a long history of this distinction. I bet the first beaver to settle here was angry when another beaver moved onto the Delmarva Peninsula. The writer claims there are positive things here. But let us not forget the "outsiders," who aren't positive. They are bad people who want to mess up Easton. They should go somewhere else. They are LGBTQA+ people.
These days, it seems socially acceptable to pick on LGBTQA+ people. Both letter writers do that. Supposedly it is OK to bully them, pass laws denying them rights and punch down on them. This attitude is unethical and dangerous. Assaults on LGBTQA+ people have risen every year, year after year, since 2017.
So, what about "Pride" as in the Pride Festival? That is a celebration of being, of being a child of God, how God or nature made you. It is not the Pride the Bible warns us about. It is not divisive. I attended the Pride Festival in Easton. No one went around hating others, yelling that others are "deviant" or "outsiders" or talking as if they were superior to others.
We need more positive community events like that. Vote out the Easton politicians who object to it.
MICHAEL DAVIS
Easton

title: New sign honors Choptank Indian Reservation in Cambridge
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
New sign honors Choptank Indian Reservation in Cambridge

 July 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 513
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Members of the Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians gathered with state officials to unveil a historical sign honoring the Choptank Indian Reservation and the indigenous ancestors who lived along the Choptank River.The sign was placed through the Maryland Roadside Historical Markers program, which is managed, in part, by the Maryland Department of Transportation. Chief Donna Abbott of the Nause-Waiwash Band thanked the state for partnering with the nonprofit group — which includes around 300 people who are descendants of the Choptank, Nanticoke and Pocomoke tribes — and led a prayer during the ceremony.
"This sign is more than just words printed on its face," Abbott said. "It is one of the first steps in telling our own story (and) preserving our history."
The reservation was occupied by Choptank people throughout the late 1700s and was the "last colonial-era reservation where the Choptank people lived together," MDOT secretary Paul Wiedefeld told attendees.
Following the unveiling of the sign, a smudging was performed around the sign. It involved the burning of herbs and the guidance of a feather meant to cleanse the surrounding area.
Julie Schablitsky, the cultural resources director for MDOT, and Mike Detmer, a Dorchester County Council member, each spoke at the ceremony.
"This is their home," Schablitsky said at the podium. "The Maryland Department of Transportation acknowledges the painful history of forced removal of native people from their territory. We honor the diverse, indigenous cultures still connected to this land."
Tom Bradshaw, a Nause-Waiwash member and the vice chair of the Maryland Commission on Indian Affairs, provided a background of the Choptank Reservation and its indigenous occupants.
In cold months, he said, their ancestors moved to the forest, and in warmer months, they would live near the river or the bay.
When English explorer John Smith came in the early 1600s, "things changed forever," Bradshaw said. Native people were pushed out of their lands and converged upon by settlers.
Bradshaw said a "remnant" of native ancestors stayed and "hid in the forests," often marrying into English or Irish families and quietly telling the history of their tribes.
Erin Kennedy, a member of the Nause-Waiwash Band who grew up on Taylor's Island, is a historian working to preserve this history. She has combed through land deeds and records to understand the history of the Choptank people and their relationships with English settlers.
She emphasized that since the Choptank people moved as the seasons changed, they helped "minimize the burdens on the environment." Kennedy said it's important to "become intentional" and take lessons from that environmentally-conscious way of life.
Transparency about land use and monitoring invasive species are two areas in which Kennedy would like to see improvement.
"Is there any consultation that we can have that can bring back the richness of biodiversity in our ecosystems?" Kennedy said in an interview with The Star Democrat. " … Any education surrounding the environment and basically how we got to this point is important."
Decades of work by historians like Kennedy and descendants of indigenous people has preserved the history of the land and its original inhabitants, Bradshaw said.
"We know we're here," he said. "We never left."
